title: Hampton overworking the audience
summary: Hampton kept repeating choruses and McRae told him to stop before the crowd's enthusiasm died.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand

blocks.x:
We used to tell Hamp -- say,
"Man, come on, Gate, you " --
He say, "Take another chorus, take
another chorus." Hamp would make you overwork if you
let him, see. We had stopped him from doing that.
Now we had something worked out on "Lady
Be Good." What we would do, like, eight choruses. That
was enough, because the tempo is up.
And what we had worked out on this
thing was enough to get over to the audience. Now
he would want us to do two more. Two more would
kill it. You understand? Two more choruses --
the people was tired of it, understand?
Three more would be too long. Like, he
used to get out there and do the "Hampton Boogie", and he'd

run up and down the stage and boom, boom. "(Inaudible)?" I say, "No, Hamp, don't do no more. Leave it die -- let it like that. Just go into the thing," you know. Go into the theme song. He stand up there and wanna do it all over again -- start from the top. By the time he got through half way, we done lost the audience. I say, "Hamp, can't you see the people's enthusiasm is gone? You're extending it (inaudible) too long?" You wanna repeat it? Go back and do three or four choruses, you know, it was a sixteen bar thing, do a couple. Do your thing (reciting notes), boom, and go out with the last chorus with the brass screaming and cut it. Go right into your theme song, come on off the stage. He'd go out there and do the whole thing over again. I say "Hamp, you're killing it." (inaudible). This is something you overdo. You really -- you're giving the public too much. They don't appreciate it.
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
